description: 🌳 Tiny & elegant JavaScript HTTP client based on the Fetch API

dimensions.label: Documentation
dimensions.summary: Can a stranger install and use this without asking you?

checks.title: README file
checks.why: The README is the landing page of your project — GitHub renders it directly under the file list.

checks.title: README depth
checks.why: A README under ~800 characters cannot cover what the project is, how to install it, and how to use it.

checks.title: Install & usage instructions
checks.message: Install + usage sections present, 70 code block(s)
checks.why: Runnable commands in the first screenful are what turn a visitor into a user.

checks.title: Open-source licence
checks.why: Without a licence, default copyright applies: legally, nobody may use your code. Companies will not touch it.

checks.title: Contributing guide
checks.why: CONTRIBUTING.md is linked automatically by GitHub whenever someone opens an issue or a pull request.

checks.title: Changelog
checks.message: No CHANGELOG file, but GitHub Releases carry written notes
checks.hint: Consider a CHANGELOG.md following https://keepachangelog.com so history is readable outside the Releases tab.
checks.why: Users upgrading across versions need to know what changed — especially what broke.

dimensions.label: Discoverability
dimensions.summary: Will anyone ever find it? Search metadata, topics, first impression.

checks.title: Repository description
checks.message: "🌳 Tiny & elegant JavaScript HTTP client based on the Fetch API" (63 chars)
checks.why: The description is the strongest ranking signal in GitHub search and the meta description Google shows.
checks.evidence: 🌳 Tiny & elegant JavaScript HTTP client based on the Fetch API

checks.title: Topics
checks.message: 11 topics: fetch, http-client, http-request, javascript, js, json, npm-package, request
checks.why: Topics are GitHub's tag system: they drive the /topics browse pages, "related repositories", and a big share of organic discovery.

checks.title: Homepage / docs link
checks.hint: Point it at your docs site, a live demo, or your project page. Even a GitHub Pages URL beats an empty field.
checks.why: The homepage field renders as a clickable link in the sidebar and is one of the few outbound signals GitHub gives you.

checks.title: README first impression
checks.message: Missing an H1 title, status badges (build, version, licence) in the first screenful
checks.hint: Structure the top of your README as: H1 → one-line pitch → badges → a 5-line usage example.
checks.why: Visitors decide in about eight seconds. A title, a one-line pitch and status badges are what they scan.

checks.title: Social preview image
checks.hint: Upload a 1280×640 image under Settings → Social preview. It is the difference between a grey box and a click on X, Slack and Discord.
checks.why: This is the og:image for every share of your repo. Without it, links render as an anonymous grey card.

checks.title: Repository name
checks.hint: Best names are 2–3 lowercase words joined by hyphens and hint at what the tool does.
checks.why: The name is the URL, the npm/PyPI package name, and the thing people have to remember and type.

dimensions.label: Engineering
dimensions.summary: CI, tests, and the hygiene that makes contributions safe to merge.

checks.title: Continuous integration
checks.message: 2 active workflow(s): CI, Copilot code review
checks.why: Without CI, every pull request is a leap of faith — for you and for the contributor.

checks.title: Test suite
checks.why: Tests are how a stranger verifies their change did not break anything — they are a contribution enabler, not just a safety net.

checks.title: .gitignore
checks.why: A missing .gitignore is how node_modules, .env files and API keys end up in git history.

checks.title: Dependency manifest & lockfile
checks.message: Manifest package.json present, no lockfile committed
checks.hint: Commit the lockfile for applications and CLIs. Libraries may skip it, but should then pin ranges deliberately.
checks.why: Reproducible installs are the difference between "works on my machine" and "works".

checks.title: Linter / formatter config
checks.hint: Pair a linter (catches bugs) with a formatter (settles style). Or use one tool that does both.
checks.why: A committed formatter config ends style debates in code review before they start.

checks.title: .editorconfig
checks.why: It makes indentation and line endings consistent across every editor, with zero setup from the contributor.

dimensions.label: Community
dimensions.summary: Is the project set up to receive help from other people?

checks.title: Issue templates
checks.hint: Add .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml and feature_request.yml. GitHub has a one-click generator under Settings → Features → Issues.
checks.why: Templates turn "it doesn't work" into a reproducible report, and save the maintainer a round trip on every single issue.

checks.title: Pull request template
checks.hint: Add .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md with: what changed, why, how it was tested, and a checklist.
checks.why: A checklist in the PR body is the cheapest way to get contributors to run the tests before asking for review.

checks.title: Code of conduct
checks.why: It sets expectations before a conflict happens and gives you something to point at when one does.

checks.title: Contributor base
checks.why: A bus factor of one is the most common reason good projects die.

checks.title: Support channel
checks.why: Without a place for questions, your issue tracker becomes one — and real bugs get buried.

dimensions.label: Maintenance
dimensions.summary: Does it look alive? Commits, releases, backlog, repo status.

checks.title: Recent commit activity
checks.why: A repo untouched for a year reads as abandoned, whether or not it is finished.

checks.title: Releases
checks.message: Latest release v2.0.2, published 4 months ago
checks.why: Tagged releases let people depend on a version instead of a moving branch.

checks.title: Issue backlog health
checks.message: No open issues or pull requests
checks.why: A backlog that grows faster than the star count signals a maintainer who has stopped responding.

checks.title: Repository status
checks.why: Archived, disabled or template repositories cannot accept the contributions your README invites.
